metadata.scope: e_aegyptus (all 125 baronies across k_blemmyia and k_egypt)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if not extracted from retrieved summary and flagged for manual check).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_sinkat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD (modern Sudanese town in Red Sea State; the Tarraconian save placed 'Baklîn' / Baqlin in this slot).
b_sinkat.etymology_analysis: Modern Beja town name in Sudan's Red Sea Hills, unattested <= 867 AD.

b_baqlin-north.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; CK3-invented directional sub-barony for the northern territory of the Beja kingdom of Baqlin (standardized as 'Nord-Baklîn').
b_baqlin-north.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound built on the medieval Beja kingdom name Baqlīn (first attested 872 AD by al-Ya'qubi).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Northern territory of the pre-867 Beja Baqlin kingdom (in-game: North Baqlin)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor North Baqlin fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Nord-Baklîn.

b_baqlin-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; CK3-invented directional sub-barony for the western hills of the Beja kingdom of Baqlin (standardized as 'West-Baklîn').
b_baqlin-west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound built on the medieval Beja kingdom name Baqlīn (first attested 872 AD by al-Ya'qubi).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Western hills of the pre-867 Beja Baqlin kingdom (in-game: West Baqlin)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor West Baqlin fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to West-Baklîn.

b_baqlin-east.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a compound <= 867 AD; CK3 directional sub-barony of Baqlin (first attested 872 AD in al-Ya'qubi).
b_baqlin-east.etymology_analysis: CK3 directional English-Arabic/Beja compound ('East Baqlin') for the eastern sub-barony of c_baqlin.

b_dherbe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD (modern/CK3 Beja locality name; the Tarraconian save placed 'Dscharîn' in this slot).
b_dherbe.etymology_analysis: Modern/CK3 Beja locality name in eastern Sudan, unattested <= 867 AD.

b_djarin.first_mention_attestation: 872 AD: 'Jārīn' (جارين, also Djarin) in al-Ya'qubi's Tarikh (and c. 891 AD in Kitab al-Buldan) as one of the six Beja kingdoms, extending from Massawa to Gash-Barka.
b_djarin.etymology_analysis: Arabic rendering (Jārīn / Djarin) of an indigenous Beja kingdom name attested in al-Ya'qubi's Tarikh (872 AD).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Zant-GUnther — Disambiguated capital foundation: Patron saint collegiate foundation dedicated by GUnther

b_khawr_baraka.first_mention_attestation: 872 AD: 'Barakāt' in al-Ya'qubi's Tarikh (i, p. 192; also Kitab al-Buldan, c. 891 AD, p. 333) as the frontier of Baqlin and a gold-mining district; later 'Nahr Baraka' in Ibn Hawqal (977 AD).
b_khawr_baraka.etymology_analysis: Arabic khawr ('seasonal watercourse') + indigenous river/region name Baraka (earliest Arabic form Barakāt in al-Ya'qubi, 872 AD, post-867).

b_kassala.first_mention_attestation: 1834 AD: Established as a Turco-Egyptian military garrison town at the foot of the Taka Mountains / Jebel Kassala.

morphemes.translation: settlement named after Jebel Kassala (etymology uncertain)

b_kassala.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese city founded in 1834 (or 1840) by Turco-Egyptian forces near Jebel Kassala; unattested in medieval or pre-867 sources.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kassâle).

b_middle_atbara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a compound toponym; CK3 English river-basin descriptor ('Middle Atbara', standardized as 'Middel-Atbara') for the middle course of the Atbara River.
b_middle_atbara.etymology_analysis: Modern directional/basin-segment descriptor attached to the Atbara River (Arabic Nahr 'Atbarah); the river itself is attested in classical antiquity as Astaboras / Astabaras.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Middle reach of the pre-867 Atbara River basin in Kassala (in-game: Middle Atbara)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Middle Atbara fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Middel-Atbara.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica 16.4.8 (c. 22 AD) as Astaboras; also Agatharchides (2nd c. BCE) as Astabaras and Ptolemy, Geographia 4.7 (c. 150 AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical hydronym Astaboras ('water of the Boras people', cf. Proto-Nubian asti 'water') is attested well before 867 AD; 'Middle' is a modern CK3 modifier.

b_to_lus.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or geographical sources; appears to be a CK3-invented or obscure Beja-style toponym.
b_to_lus.etymology_analysis: Unattested toponym using the Beja feminine prefix to- with an opaque or invented second element Lus.

b_qataa.first_mention_attestation: 872 AD: 'Qiṭā'a' / 'Qatā' in al-Ya'qubi's Tarikh (and c. 891 AD in Kitab al-Buldan) as one of the six medieval Beja kingdoms between Aswan and Massawa.

morphemes.translation: indigenous Beja polity name (or Arabic qit'a 'section/tract')

b_qataa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic rendering (Qiṭā'a / Qatā) of a Beja kingdom name (rendered 'Katâ' in raw data), first attested by al-Ya'qubi in 872 AD (post-867).

b_marya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; ethnonym of the Tigre-speaking Marya (Tigre: ማርያ) of the Anseba valley in western Eritrea, documented in post-medieval/19th-century sources.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of a Tigre-speaking pastoralist group

b_marya.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Marya people of western Eritrea (Anseba valley), unattested before 867 AD.

b_showak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; modern Sudanese town (Arabic: الشواك, al-Shuwāk) on the Atbara River in Al-Qadarif State.

morphemes.translation: thorny scrub / acacia thorns (pl. of shawk) or local place name

b_showak.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic town name (al-Shuwāk, standardized as 'Schowach' in raw data) with no pre-867 attestation.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Schowach).

b_gash.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; modern Sudanese/Arabic hydronym (القاش, al-Qāsh) for the lower course and inland delta of the Mereb River.
b_gash.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the seasonal Gash River (upper course Mereb River) reaching Kassala; unattested in sources <= 867 AD.

b_showak_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a compound <= 867 AD; CK3 directional sub-barony of Showak.
b_showak_south.etymology_analysis: CK3 directional compound ('South Showak') for the southern sub-barony of c_showak.

b_wolqayt.first_mention_attestation: c. 1468–1478 AD: Attested in Ethiopian traditions/chronicles of Emperor Baeda Maryam I (an 8th/9th-century Aksumite inscription of Hatsani Daniel mentions WYLQ, only tentatively identified with Welkait).

morphemes.translation: regional toponym in northwestern Ethiopia (etymology uncertain)

b_wolqayt.etymology_analysis: Toponym in northwestern Ethiopia (Tigray/Amhara borderland) firmly attested from the 15th century (reign of Baeda Maryam I); an earlier Aksumite inscription (Hatsani Daniel, 8th–9th c.) mentions WYLQ, whose identification with Welkait is tentative.

b_wad_abu_nahl.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; modern Sudanese Arabic settlement/wadi name in Al-Qadarif State.

morphemes.translation: father of bees (personal/tribal name or 'place of bees')

b_wad_abu_nahl.etymology_analysis: Modern Sudanese Arabic toponym ('Wad Abu Nahl') in Al-Qadarif State with no medieval or pre-867 attestation.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Wad Abu Nahl (constituent holding of Wolkaît)

b_wegera.first_mention_attestation: c. 1316–1332 AD: Attested in the Ge'ez chronicle of Emperor Amda Seyon I (Glorious Victories) recording his western campaigns in Gojjam and Wogera.

morphemes.translation: highland district north of Gondar (etymology uncertain)

b_wegera.etymology_analysis: Historic Ethiopian highland province north of Gondar, first attested in the 14th-century chronicles of Amda Seyon I (post-867).

b_allaqi.first_mention_attestation: 855 AD (241 AH): 'Wādī al-ʿAllāqī' (وادي العلاقي) attested in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (pp. 379–382) and al-Tabari's Tarikh for al-Qummi's Abbasid campaign against the Beja.

morphemes.translation: the Allaqi (possibly from Arabic 'alaq / 'alāqa or Arabized Beja/Egyptian substrate)

b_allaqi.etymology_analysis: Arabic hydronym/toponym for the major Eastern Desert gold-mining wadi, attested in 855 AD during the Abbasid-Beja conflict (<= 867 AD), with an earlier Pharaonic name Akuyati.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Kuban Stela of Ramesses II (19th Dynasty, c. 1279–1213 BCE), recording Egyptian gold-mining and well-digging in Akuyati.
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Egyptian name (ꜣkꜣyt / Akuyati / Ikaita) for the Wadi Allaqi gold-mining region.

b_derahib.first_mention_attestation: Modern/post-867 Beja-Arabic toponym for the medieval Islamic mining town (al-'Allaqi, 9th–12th c. AD) in upper Wadi Allaqi.
b_derahib.etymology_analysis: Modern local name for the ruins of the 9th–12th century Islamic mining city of al-'Allaqi in upper Wadi Allaqi; identified by CeRDO archaeologists with Ptolemaic Berenice Panchrysos.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica 16.4.10 (c. 22 AD) and Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 6.34 (77 AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Identified by Italian CeRDO expeditions as Ptolemaic Berenice Panchrysos ('All-Golden Berenice'), though the identification remains debated.

b_haimur.first_mention_attestation: Toponym 'Haimur' is unattested <= 867 AD; archaeological gold-mining workings at Wadi Haimur date to the New Kingdom (1550–1070 BCE) and early Arab period.

morphemes.translation: local mine and wadi name (etymology uncertain)

b_haimur.etymology_analysis: Historic gold mine in the central Wadi Allaqi belt with Pharaonic and early Islamic workings, but the toponym Haimur itself is unattested before 867 AD.

b_aydhab.first_mention_attestation: 855 AD (241 AH): 'ʿAydhāb' (عيذاب) attested in al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan (pp. 379–382) as the Red Sea port provisioning al-Qummi's 855 AD Beja campaign.

morphemes.translation: medieval Red Sea port name (etymology uncertain)

b_aydhab.etymology_analysis: Important early Islamic Red Sea port in the Halaib Triangle, attested in 855 AD (<= 867 AD) in al-Baladhuri's account of the Abbasid expedition against the Beja.

b_lower_odib.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; CK3-invented directional descriptor ('Lower Odib', standardized as 'Nider-Aidâp') for the lower coastal plain of Wadi Odib near 'Aydhab.
b_lower_odib.etymology_analysis: CK3-invented English directional descriptor ('Lower Odib', standardized as 'Nider-Aidâp') referring to the lower Wadi Odib coastal plain; unattested <= 867 AD.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Lower coastal plain of the pre-867 Wadi Odib near Aidhab (in-game: Lower Odib)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Lower Odib fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Nider-Aidâp.

b_gebeit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD (modern Sudanese town/gold-mining site in Red Sea State; the Tarraconian save placed 'Nakîs' / Naqis in this slot).
b_gebeit.etymology_analysis: Modern Beja town and mining locality in Sudan's Red Sea Hills, unattested <= 867 AD.

b_wadi_odib.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; modern Sudanese/Beja wadi toponym in Red Sea State.
b_wadi_odib.etymology_analysis: Arabic wādī + indigenous Beja toponym Odib in northeastern Sudan; unattested in medieval or pre-867 sources.

b_naqis-north.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; CK3-invented directional sub-barony for the northern district of Naqis (standardized as 'Nord-Nakîs').
b_naqis-north.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound built on the medieval Beja kingdom name Naqīs (first attested 872 AD by al-Ya'qubi).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Northern gold-mining district of the pre-867 Wadi Allaqi (in-game: North Naqis)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor North Naqis fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Nord-Nakîs.

b_naqis-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a compound <= 867 AD; CK3 directional sub-barony of Naqis (first attested 872 AD in al-Ya'qubi).
b_naqis-south.etymology_analysis: CK3 directional compound ('South Naqis') for the southern sub-barony of c_naqis.

b_khawr_nubt.first_mention_attestation: Toponym 'Khawr Nubt' is unattested in medieval texts <= 867 AD (archaeological site in Sudan's Red Sea Hills with 9th-10th century Islamic tombstones).
b_khawr_nubt.etymology_analysis: Arabic-Beja hydronym ('Wadi Nubt') for an archaeological valley in Sudan's Red Sea Hills; unattested by name <= 867 AD.

b_wadi_amur.first_mention_attestation: Toponym 'Wadi Amur' is unattested <= 867 AD (seasonal watercourse in Sudan's Red Sea Hills; Blemmyean-era remains at Alitia nearby).
b_wadi_amur.etymology_analysis: Arabic-Beja hydronym ('Wadi Amur') for a seasonal watercourse in Sudan's Red Sea Hills; unattested by name <= 867 AD.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Karlmunster — Disambiguated capital foundation: Collegiate minster church established by Karl

b_upper_amur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; CK3-invented directional descriptor ('Upper Amur', standardized as 'Ober-Amûr') for the upper basin of Wadi Amur.
b_upper_amur.etymology_analysis: Modern directional descriptor ('Upper Amur', standardized as 'Ober-Amûr') for the upper reach of Wadi Amur; unattested <= 867 AD.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Upper basin reach of the pre-867 Wadi Amur in Nubia (in-game: Upper Amur)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Upper Amur fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Ober-Amûr.

b_aswan.first_mention_attestation: c. 2300 BCE, Old Kingdom Egyptian 'Swenet' (swn.t) in First Cataract frontier inscriptions (later Aramaic 'Swn' 5th c. BCE, Greek 'Syene' c. 450 BCE in Herodotus).
b_aswan.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian Swenet (swn.t, 'trade/market'), reflecting its role as the southern frontier trading post at the First Cataract; passed via Greek Syene and Coptic Souan (ⲥⲟⲩⲁⲛ) into Arabic Aswān.

b_udfu.first_mention_attestation: c. 2400 BCE, Old Kingdom Egyptian 'Djeba' (ḏbꜣ) and 'Behdet' (bḥdt) in 5th/6th Dynasty records (later Coptic 'Atbō' / 'Tbō', Arabic 'Udfū').
b_udfu.etymology_analysis: Arabic Udfū (Idfu) derives directly through Sahidic Coptic Tbō (ⲧⲃⲱ) and Bohairic Atbō (ⲁⲧⲃⲱ) from Ancient Egyptian Djeba (ḏbꜣ).

b_zarnikh.first_mention_attestation: 1816 CE (1231 AH), cited in Egyptian cadastral records (Muhammad Ramzi) when Jazirat al-Riqiyya was separated from Zarnikh and al-Kilabiya.
b_zarnikh.etymology_analysis: Arabic Zarnīkh (زرنيخ, 'arsenic/orpiment', ultimately from Persian zarnīkh 'gold-colored'), a village in Esna district (Luxor Governorate) locally associated with mineral deposits.

b_aswan-west.first_mention_attestation: Modern directional/administrative designation (Arabic Gharb Aswān) for the west bank of the Nile opposite Aswan; no attestation of this name <= 867 AD.
b_aswan-west.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic directional compound Gharb Aswān ('West Aswan'). In antiquity, the adjacent First Cataract island and west-bank nexus was Elephantine (Egyptian ꜣbw).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Pharaonic and Roman island fortress Elephantine on the Nile (in-game: West Aswan)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Modern administrative sector West Aswan fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to classical island fortress Elephantine.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Old Kingdom Egyptian inscriptions at Elephantine (ꜣbw, c. 2600 BCE); Greek Elephantínē.
older_name_by_867.notes: Elephantine (Egyptian ꜣbw) was the ancient island fortress and First Cataract administrative center adjacent to modern West Aswan.

b_asyut.first_mention_attestation: c. 2100 BCE, First Intermediate Period/Middle Kingdom Egyptian 'Zawty' (zꜣwtj) in nomarch tombs at Asyut (later Coptic 'Siōout', Arabic 'Suyūṭ' 846 AD / 'Asyūṭ').
b_asyut.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian zꜣwtj ('guardian' of the northern approach of Upper Egypt), through Coptic Siōout (ⲥⲓⲟⲟⲩⲧ) into Arabic Suyūṭ / Asyūṭ.

b_bawit.first_mention_attestation: c. 385 CE, foundation of the Monastery of Apa Apollo at Coptic 'Pavēt' / 'Paouēt' (ⲡⲁⲩⲏⲧ).
b_bawit.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bāwīṭ derives directly from Coptic Pavēt / Paouēt (ⲡⲁⲩⲏⲧ, 'the assembly/monastery'), referring to the major Coptic monastery founded by Apa Apollo c. 385 CE.

b_ikhmin.first_mention_attestation: c. 450 BCE, Herodotus 'Khemmis' (Χέμμις), from Egyptian 'Khent-Min' (ḫnt-mnw); Coptic 'Khmin' / 'Shmin' (ⳉⲙⲓⲙ / ϣⲙⲓⲛ), Arabic 'Akhmīm'.
b_ikhmin.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian Khent-Min ('shrine of Min'), yielding Greek Khemmis, Akhmimic Coptic Khmin (ⳉⲙⲓⲙ), and Arabic Akhmīm / Ikhmīm.

b_ibshaya.first_mention_attestation: After 312 BCE, Egyptian village 'Psoi' (Coptic ⲡⲥⲟⲓ) on which Ptolemais Hermiou was founded; attested in Arabic as 'Ibshāya' (أبشاية) by Ibn Khordadbeh in 846 CE.
b_ibshaya.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic Ibshāya (أبشاية, attested 846 CE) derives phonologically from Coptic Psoi (ⲡⲥⲟⲓ), the indigenous name of Ptolemais Hermiou (modern El Mansha).

b_al-bahnasa.first_mention_attestation: 846 CE, attested as 'al-Bahnasā' in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik; derived from Coptic 'Pemdje' (ⲡⲉⲙϫⲉ) / Egyptian 'Per-Medjed' (pr-mḏd).
b_al-bahnasa.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Bahnasā (attested by 846 CE) evolved phonologically from Coptic Pemdje (ⲡⲉⲙϫⲉ), itself from Ancient Egyptian Per-Medjed (known in Greek as Oxyrhynchus).

b_ahnas.first_mention_attestation: c. 2100 BCE, First Intermediate Period (9th/10th Dynasty) capital 'Henen-nesut' (ḥnn-nswt); later Coptic 'Hnes' (ϩⲛⲏⲥ) and early Arabic 'Ahnās'.
b_ahnas.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian Henen-nesut ('Child of the King'), passing through Coptic Hnes (ϩⲛⲏⲥ) into early Egyptian Arabic Ahnās (modern Ihnasya el-Madina).

b_ihrit.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE, attested as 'Ihrīt' in Ibn Mammati's Qawanin al-Dawawin (and al-Nabulsi 1245 CE) in Fayyum.
b_ihrit.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic Ihrīt / Baṭn Ihrīt (attested c. 1200 CE) is the name of the village and ruins (Kharabet Ihrit) on the site of ancient Theadelphia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemaic papyri from Theadelphia (c. 280 BCE); abandoned in the 4th century CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Kharabet Ihrit / Batn Ihrit marks the archaeological site of Greco-Roman Theadelphia.

b_qus.first_mention_attestation: c. 2200 BCE, late Old Kingdom/First Intermediate Period Egyptian 'Gesa' (gsꜣ) in governor stelae at Naqada; later Coptic 'Kōs' (ⲕⲱⲥ) and Arabic 'Qūṣ'.
b_qus.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qūṣ derives through Coptic Kōs (ⲕⲱⲥ / ⲕⲱⲥ ⲃⲉⲣⲃⲓⲣ) from Ancient Egyptian Gesa (gsꜣ), known in Greco-Roman times as Apollinopolis Parva.

b_huw.first_mention_attestation: c. 2000 BCE, Middle Kingdom Egyptian 'Hut-Sekhem' (ḥwt-sḫm), abbreviated 'Hu', Coptic 'Hō' / 'Hou' (ϩⲱ / ϩⲟⲩ), Arabic 'Hū' / 'Huw'.
b_huw.etymology_analysis: Abbreviated from Ancient Egyptian Hut-Sekhem ('Mansion of the Sistrum') to Hu, passing through Coptic Hō/Hou (ϩⲱ/ϩⲟⲩ) into Arabic Hū (Huw).

b_faw.first_mention_attestation: 336–337 CE, Coptic 'Pbow' / 'Pboou' (ⲡⲃⲟⲟⲩ), founded as the administrative center of St. Pachomius's monastic Koinonia.
b_faw.etymology_analysis: Arabic Fāw (Fāw Qiblī, 'Southern Faw') derives directly from Coptic Pbow / Pboou (ⲡⲃⲟⲟⲩ), site of the major 4th-century Pachomian monastery.

b_qina.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 CE, Ptolemy's Geography (4.5.72) as Greek 'Kainē' (Καινή / Kainē polis, 'new city'); later Arabic 'Qinā'.
b_qina.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qinā derives directly from Greco-Roman Kainē / Kainēpolis (Καινή πόλις, 'New City'), later also called Maximianopolis.

b_armant.first_mention_attestation: c. 2000 BCE, Middle Kingdom Egyptian 'Iuny-Montu' (jwn.w-n-mnṯ.w); later Greek 'Hermonthis', Coptic 'Ermont' (ⲉⲣⲙⲟⲛⲧ), Arabic 'Armant'.
b_armant.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian Iuny-Montu ('Heliopolis of Montu'), passing through Coptic Ermont / Rmont (ⲉⲣⲙⲟⲛⲧ / ⲣ̄ⲙⲟⲛⲧ) into Arabic Armant.

b_al-ushmunain.first_mention_attestation: c. 2400 BCE, Old Kingdom Egyptian 'Khemenu' (ḫmnw, 'Eight'); later Coptic 'Shmūn' (ϣⲙⲟⲩⲛ) and Arabic 'al-Ushmūnayn' (attested 846 CE in Ibn Khordadbeh).
b_al-ushmunain.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Egyptian Khemenu ('Eight', referring to the Ogdoad), through Coptic Shmūn (ϣⲙⲟⲩⲛ) into Arabic al-Ushmūnayn (with Arabic dual ending -ayn).

b_ansina.first_mention_attestation: 130 CE, founded by Emperor Hadrian as 'Antinoöpolis' (Ἀντινόου πόλις); Coptic 'Antinōou' (ⲁⲛⲧⲓⲛⲱⲟⲩ), Arabic 'Anṣinā' (attested 846 CE in Ibn Khordadbeh).
b_ansina.etymology_analysis: Founded by Hadrian in 130 CE as Antinoöpolis in honor of Antinous; passed through Coptic Antinōou (ⲁⲛⲧⲓⲛⲱⲟⲩ) into early Arabic Anṣinā (modern Sheikh Ibada).

b_manfalut.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE, medieval Arabic 'Manfalūṭ' (منفلوط) in Ibn Mammati/Yaqut; derived from Coptic 'Manbalot' (ⲙⲁⲛⲃⲁⲗⲟⲧ), though no dated pre-867 attestation is confirmed.
b_manfalut.etymology_analysis: Arabic Manfalūṭ derives from Coptic Manbalot (ⲙⲁⲛⲃⲁⲗⲟⲧ, 'place of pelts/skins').

b_al-bahriya.first_mention_attestation: Late medieval/modern Arabic 'al-Wāḥāt al-Baḥriyya' ('the Northern Oases'); in 867 CE and earlier medieval Arabic it was known as 'Wāḥ al-Bahnasā'.
b_al-bahriya.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic geographical name al-Wāḥāt al-Baḥriyya ('the Northern Oases'); earlier known in Egyptian as Djesdjes and Wahet-Mehtyt, in Roman times as Oasis Parva, and in early Islamic times as Wāḥ al-Bahnasā.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Middle Kingdom scarab mentioning 'ḏsḏs' (Djesdjes, c. 2000 BCE); Pliny 'Oasis Parva' (45 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in antiquity as Djesdjes / Wahet-Mehtyt / Oasis Parva and in early Islamic times as Wah al-Bahnasa.

b_bawiti.first_mention_attestation: Modern/late medieval Arabic 'al-Bāwīṭī' (الباويطي) from Coptic 'Paouēt' (ⲡⲁⲩⲏⲧ); no dated pre-867 textual attestation for the settlement name in Bahariya.
b_bawiti.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Bāwīṭī derives from Coptic Paouēt (ⲡⲁⲩⲏⲧ, 'assembly/monastery'). Although 26th Dynasty tombs exist nearby at Qarat Qasr Salim, no dated pre-867 attestation of the settlement name Bawiti is established.

b_al-harra.first_mention_attestation: Modern Arabic village name 'al-Ḥārra' (الحارة) in Bahariya Oasis; no attestation <= 867 CE.
b_al-harra.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥārra, a modern village in the eastern part of Bahariya Oasis.

b_mut.first_mention_attestation: c. 100 CE, Roman-era capital of Dakhla Oasis attested in Greek as 'Mōthis' (Μῶθις) and in Egyptian as 'Mt' (Mut).
b_mut.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mūṭ (موط) derives from Greco-Roman Mōthis (Μῶθις) and Ancient Egyptian Mt, named after the goddess Mut.

b_tunayda.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE, attested as 'Ḥayz Tunayda' (حيز تنيدة) in Ibn Mammati's Qawanin al-Dawawin.
b_tunayda.etymology_analysis: Village at the eastern entrance of Dakhla Oasis, first attested in medieval Arabic cadastral sources (Ibn Mammati c. 1200 CE) as Ḥayz Tunayda.

b_al-qasr-dakhla.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th century CE (c. 1175–1200 CE), fortified Islamic town of Qasr ad-Dakhla founded by the Ayyubids over a Roman fort.
b_al-qasr-dakhla.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qaṣr ('the Fortress', from Latin castrum), founded by the Ayyubids in the late 12th century on the ruins of a Roman fort.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman military fort beneath Al-Qasr (c. 1st–4th century CE, identified in local/Arabic historiography with Roman Tacastra).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ayyubid Al-Qasr was built directly over the remains of a Roman-period fort.

b_al-farafra.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE, attested as 'al-Farfarūn' (الفرفرون) in Ibn Mammati's Qawanin al-Dawawin.

morphemes.translation: the bubbling/fizzy (springs), broken plural of farfar

b_al-farafra.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Farāfra (medieval al-Farfarūn, attested c. 1200 CE), derived from farfar ('fizzy/bubbling') referring to its springs; in Pharaonic times it was called Ta-ihet ('Land of the Cow').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pharaonic Egyptian inscriptions naming 'Ta-ihet' (tꜣ-jḥt, 'Land of the Cow').
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Egyptian name for Farafra Oasis.

b_kharga.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE, medieval Arabic 'al-Khārija' ('the outer', calque of Greek hē Exōterō); anciently 'Hebet' / 'Hibis' / 'Oasis Magna'.
b_kharga.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Khārija ('the outer') is a semantic calque of Greek hē Exōterō ('the outer [oasis]'), replacing earlier Egyptian Hebet / Hibis and Coptic Ouah en-Hib.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Temple of Hibis (c. 500 BCE, Persian/27th Dynasty); Greek 'He Exotero' and Latin 'Oasis Magna'.
older_name_by_867.notes: Anciently known as Hebet/Hibis and Oasis Magna.

b_baris.first_mention_attestation: Arabic 'Bārīs' (باريس) from Coptic 'Parēs' (ⲡⲁⲣⲏⲥ, 'the one of the south'); no dated pre-867 textual attestation of the name Baris/Parēs is confirmed.
b_baris.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bārīs derives from Coptic Parēs (ⲡⲁⲣⲏⲥ, 'the one of the south'), located at the southern end of Kharga Oasis near the Roman temple of Dush (ancient Kysis).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman temple of Isis and Serapis at Dush (ancient Kysis), built 117 CE.
older_name_by_867.notes: Dush (ancient Kysis) is the major Greco-Roman site 23 km from modern Baris.

b_alexandria.first_mention_attestation: 331 BCE, founded by Alexander the Great as 'Alexándreia' (Ἀλεξάνδρεια); Arabic 'al-Iskandariyya'.
b_alexandria.etymology_analysis: Named after its founder Alexander the Great in 331 BCE (Greek Alexándreia, Arabic al-Iskandariyya).

b_al-hamam.first_mention_attestation: Modern Arabic 'al-Ḥammām' (الحمام) in Matrouh Governorate; no attestation <= 867 CE.
b_al-hamam.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥammām ('the bath' or 'the pigeons', associated locally with Roman baths/cisterns or wild pigeons). The ancient Greek town of Cheimo lay in its vicinity.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Stadiasmus Maris Magni (c. 3rd–4th century CE) mentioning 'Cheimo' (Χειμὼ).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek coastal town Cheimo located in the vicinity of El Hamam.

b_wadi_natrun.first_mention_attestation: Medieval/modern Arabic 'Wādī al-Naṭrūn' ('Valley of Natron'); in 867 CE and antiquity it was known as 'Scetis', 'Shihēt' (Ϣⲓϩⲏⲧ), and 'Nitria'.
b_wadi_natrun.etymology_analysis: Arabic Wādī al-Naṭrūn ('Valley of Natron'), referring to its alkaline natron lakes; known in antiquity as Sekhet-hemat ('Field of Salt'), in Coptic as Shihēt (Ϣⲓϩⲏⲧ), and in Greek as Scetis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Christian monastic settlement of Scetis by St. Macarius (c. 330 CE); also Pharaonic 'Eloquent Peasant' (c. 1900 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Scetis / Shihēt in Late Antiquity and the early Islamic period.

b_siwa.first_mention_attestation: 15th century CE, Arabic 'Sīwa' (سيوة) in al-Maqrizi (possibly local 1203 CE manuscript); in 867 CE it was known as 'Santariyya' (سنترية) and anciently 'Ammonium'.

morphemes.translation: Siwa (possibly from Berber tribal name swh or asiwan 'falcon')

b_siwa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sīwa (from Berber Isiwan / Sali, etymology debated: Berber tribal name swh, asiwan 'falcon', or Coptic soouh 'oasis') replaced earlier Islamic Santariyya and classical Ammonium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus (c. 450 BCE) 'Ammonium'; early Arabic geographers (9th c. CE) 'Santariyya'.
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 CE the oasis was known to Arab geographers as Santariyya.

b_ain_al-gharbi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE; generic Arabic topographic name ('the Western Spring') used in CK3 for Siwa.
b_ain_al-gharbi.etymology_analysis: Arabic ʿAyn al-Gharbī ('the Western Spring'), a generic descriptive hydronym unattested in pre-867 historical records.

b_qara.first_mention_attestation: Modern Arabic 'al-Qāra' / 'Qārat Umm al-Ṣaghīr' (قارة أم الصغير); no attestation of this name <= 867 CE.
b_qara.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qāra ('the hillock/mesa'), referring to the rocky hilltop fortress of Qārat Umm al-Ṣaghīr northeast of Siwa.

b_sullum.first_mention_attestation: 12th century CE (c. 1154 CE), Arabic 'ʿAqaba as-Sallūm' ('graded ascent / ladder pass'); anciently 'Catabathmus Maior' (Polybius, 162 BCE).
b_sullum.etymology_analysis: Arabic as-Sallūm (from ʿAqaba as-Sallūm, 'graded ascent', attested in the 12th century), semantically mirroring Greek Katabathmós ('descent').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Polybius, World History 31.18.9 (162 BCE) mentioning Catabathmus; Strabo and Ptolemy.
older_name_by_867.notes: Anciently known as Catabathmus Maior (with harbor Plynos Limen and fort Tetrapyrgia).

b_qasr_ash-shams.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE in Sallum/Marmarica (note: Qaṣr al-Shamʿ was Babylon Fortress in Cairo).
b_qasr_ash-shams.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qaṣr ash-Shams ('Castle of the Sun'), unattested as a historical settlement in the Sallum region <= 867 CE.

b_kanais_al-hadid.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources <= 867 CE; Arabic compound ('Churches of Iron'), possibly related to Ras el-Kanayis.
b_kanais_al-hadid.etymology_analysis: Arabic Kanāʾis al-Ḥadīd ('Churches of Iron'), unattested in pre-867 historical sources.

b_badi.first_mention_attestation: 637 AD (recorded by 9th-century historian al-Tabari): Caliph Umar exiled the poet Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi to the Red Sea port of Badi' (Bāḍiʿ), later mentioned in the 724–734 AD treaty between Egypt and the Beja.

morphemes.translation: medieval Red Sea port on the island of al-Rīḥ (Er Rih); of uncertain/pre-Islamic or Arabic root

b_badi.etymology_analysis: Bāḍiʿ was the earliest Arab-established port on the Sudanese Red Sea coast (on the island of Er Rih near the Gulf of Aqiq), flourishing c. 600–1100 AD and attested in early Islamic historiography from 637 AD onward. The etymology of Bāḍiʿ is uncertain, possibly from an Arabic root or a local Beja/Red Sea coastal name.

b_ka'abir.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical, geographical, or archaeological sources for the Badi / Aqiq / Beja Red Sea coast; appears in Crusader Kings III as an unoccupied holding in c_badi.

morphemes.translation: unattested toponym in the Badi–Aqiq region (possibly a corruption or variant of a Beja clan or local Arabic name, cf. Kubir noted by al-Ya'qubi)

b_ka'abir.etymology_analysis: No historical settlement named Ka'abir is attested in the Badi/Aqiq region of the Sudanese Red Sea coast. It is left empty in barony_resolutions.json as an unoccupied holding and lacks pre-867 attestation.

b_tokar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 19th century (developed during Ottoman-Egyptian cotton cultivation in the Khor Baraka delta under Mumtaz Pasha in the 1860s and prominent in the 1883–1891 Mahdist War); unattested by 867 AD.

morphemes.translation: town in the Khor Baraka delta, Red Sea State, Sudan

b_tokar.etymology_analysis: Tokar is a modern agricultural town in the Khor Baraka delta of southeastern Sudan whose recorded history begins in the 19th century with Ottoman-Egyptian cotton cultivation and the Mahdist War. Its name is of local Beja/Sudanese origin with no pre-867 attestation.

b_akik.first_mention_attestation: The Arabic name Aqiq (ʿAqīq) for the Sudanese Red Sea town and bay is attested in medieval/modern Islamic and colonial sources, with no explicit pre-867 attestation of the Arabic toponym itself.
b_akik.etymology_analysis: Aqiq (also spelled Akik) is a coastal settlement on the Gulf of Aqiq in Sudan. While classical scholars (Crowfoot 1911; Oxford Classical Dictionary) tentatively identify the Aqiq area with Ptolemais Theron, surface surveys found only Islamic-era pottery and the Arabic name Aqiq is not attested by 867 AD.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pithom Stele of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (c. 270–264 BC) and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Tentatively identified with Aqiq by J. W. Crowfoot and the Oxford Classical Dictionary, though the exact archaeological identification remains debated.

b_bazin.first_mention_attestation: Late 9th century AD (c. 872–891 AD): 'Kingdom of Bazin' (بازين) first recorded by Arab historian al-Ya'qubi among the six medieval Beja kingdoms between Aswan and Massawa.

morphemes.translation: medieval Beja kingdom; associated with the Kunama people, called 'Bazen' by Abyssinians

b_bazin.etymology_analysis: Bazin was one of the six medieval Beja polities first described by al-Ya'qubi (late 9th century AD, c. 872–891 AD) as being at war with Alodia. The name corresponds to 'Bazen', the Abyssinian ethnonym for the Kunama who inhabited part of the kingdom; its earliest written attestation postdates 867 AD by a few years.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Wiltrudstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Wiltrud

b_suakin.first_mention_attestation: 10th century AD (c. 940 AD): 'Sawākin' first mentioned by name by al-Hamdani (d. 945 AD), who describes it as already an ancient town.

morphemes.translation: at the market (locative of sūq 'market'); Arabicized as Sawākin

b_suakin.etymology_analysis: The Beja name for Suakin is Oosook, likely borrowed from Arabic sūq ('market'), whose Beja locative form isukib ('at the market') is the probable source of Arabic Sawākin / Suakin. First attested by name in the 10th century by al-Hamdani.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 AD): Evangelon Portus ('Port of Good Hope'), lying on a circular island at the end of a long inlet.
older_name_by_867.notes: Modern scholars and archaeologists identify Ptolemy's 2nd-century Evangelon Portus with the island harbour of Suakin.

b_dungunab.first_mention_attestation: First documented in modern scientific and geographic literature in the late 19th to early 20th century (e.g., Cyril Crossland, 1911); unattested by 867 AD.

morphemes.translation: coastal bay and settlement on the Sudanese Red Sea coast

b_dungunab.etymology_analysis: Dungunab (also Dongonab) is a coastal village and bay north of Port Sudan in Red Sea State, Sudan. Of local Beja/Sudanese origin, it is unattested in historical sources prior to 867 AD.

b_cairo.first_mention_attestation: 969 AD: Founded by the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli as al-Manṣūriyya and renamed al-Qāhira ('The Victorious', whence Cairo) in 973 AD by Caliph al-Mu'izz.

morphemes.translation: the Vanquisher / the Victorious (epithet of Mars, al-Najm al-Qāhir)

b_cairo.etymology_analysis: Cairo (Arabic al-Qāhira, 'The Victorious') was founded in 969 AD by the Fatimid Caliphate just north of Fustat, reportedly named after the planet Mars (al-Qāhir) rising at the time of its foundation. Both Fustat (641 AD) and Roman Babylon Fortress (c. 300 AD) predate it on the site.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Babylon Fortress built c. 300 AD by Emperor Diocletian; Al-Fustat founded 641 AD by 'Amr ibn al-'As immediately after the Muslim conquest of Egypt.
older_name_by_867.notes: Al-Fustat (641 AD) was the Islamic capital of Egypt adjacent to the Roman Babylon Fortress (c. 300 AD) before Fatimid Cairo was founded to its north in 969 AD.

b_quzlum.first_mention_attestation: Early 2nd century AD: Greek 'Klŷsma' (Κλῦσμα) first recorded in Lucian's Alexander Pseudomantis and Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD); Arabized as al-Qulzum after 641 AD.

morphemes.translation: surf, waves that break (whence Coptic Peklousma and Arabic al-Qulzum)

b_quzlum.etymology_analysis: Quzlum (al-Qulzum) is the Arabicized form of Ancient Greek Klŷsma ('surf, waves that break'), a major Roman and early Islamic Red Sea port at the head of the Gulf of Suez (giving the Red Sea its medieval Arabic name Baḥr al-Qulzum).

b_atfih.first_mention_attestation: c. 2000 BC: Ancient Egyptian Per-nebet tep-ihu / Tp-jḥw (attested in the Tomb of 'Ip at Atfih), evolving into Coptic Petpēh / Tpēh and Arabic Aṭfīḥ.

morphemes.translation: the first of the cows (referring to Hathor / Hesat)

b_atfih.etymology_analysis: Atfih (Arabic Aṭfīḥ) derives directly via Coptic Petpēh / Tpēh from Ancient Egyptian Tp-jḥw ('first of the cows'), a sacred epithet of the goddess Hathor; it was also called Aphroditopolis by the Greeks.

b_hulwan-cairo.first_mention_attestation: 689 AD: Umayyad governor 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan established Helwan (Ḥulwān) as the temporary capital of Egypt during a plague in Fustat (with proposed Ancient Egyptian ancestor Hor-Ain-Anne / Ain-an attested c. 700 BC).

morphemes.language: Arabic (possibly from Coptic Halwan / Egyptian Ain-an)
morphemes.translation: uncertain; either from Egyptian Ain-an ('Spring of the Fish') via Coptic Halwan, or named by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan after Hulwan in Iran

b_hulwan-cairo.etymology_analysis: Helwan (Ḥulwān) was made the Umayyad capital of Egypt in 689 AD by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan. Scholars derive the name either from Ancient Egyptian Ain-an ('Spring of the Fish', referring to its sulfur springs) via Coptic Halwan, or from the Persian city of Hulwan.

b_al-fayyum.first_mention_attestation: Late Egyptian (c. 1300 BC): pꜣ-ym ('the sea/lake'), passing into Coptic Phiom / Peiom and Arabic al-Fayyūm (older city site founded c. 2500 BC as Shedet / Crocodilopolis).

natural_proper_name.name: pꜣ-ym / Phiom ('the sea/lake', referring to Lake Moeris)

b_al-fayyum.etymology_analysis: Al-Fayyum derives via Coptic Phiom / Peiom from Late Egyptian pꜣ-ym ('the sea' or 'the lake'), a reference to the nearby Lake Moeris (Birket Qarun). The city itself dates back to the Old Kingdom as Shedet (Greek Crocodilopolis / Arsinoë).

b_tirsa.first_mention_attestation: 1177 AD: Listed as 'Tirsā' (ترسا) in the Fayyum province (al-Fayyūmiyya) in Ibn Mammati's Qawānīn al-Dawāwīn (al-Rawk al-Ṣalāḥī cadastral survey).

morphemes.translation: village in Sennuris district, Faiyum Governorate (distinct from Tirsa in Giza)

b_tirsa.etymology_analysis: Tirsa in the Fayyum (Sennuris district) is first attested in the 1177 AD Ayyubid cadastral survey (al-Rawk al-Ṣalāḥī) recorded by Ibn Mammati. Unlike the homonymous Tirsa in Giza (Coptic Tersō), the Fayyum village has no pre-867 attestation.

b_iqna.first_mention_attestation: 1177 AD: Recorded as 'Munyat Aqnā' (منية أقنى) in the Fayyum province in Ibn Mammati's Qawānīn al-Dawāwīn (al-Rawk al-Ṣalāḥī) and later in Ibn al-Ji'an's al-Tuḥfa al-Saniyya.

morphemes.translation: historical village in the Fayyum (shortened from Munyat Aqnā)

b_iqna.etymology_analysis: Iqna corresponds to the historical Fayyum village of Munyat Aqnā (منية أقنى), first attested in Ibn Mammati's late 12th-century Qawānīn al-Dawāwīn (1177 AD survey) and later subsumed into al-Mushrik. No pre-867 attestation exists.

b_gizeh.first_mention_attestation: 642 AD (21 AH): Founded as a garrison/city on the west bank of the Nile by the Rashidun Muslim army following the conquest of Egypt.

morphemes.language: Arabic (or Middle Persian diz / Egyptian r-gs-ḥr)
morphemes.translation: edge, side of the valley (per al-Maqrizi); alternatively Middle Persian diz ('fortress') or Egyptian r-gs-ḥr ('on the side of the pyramid')

b_gizeh.etymology_analysis: Giza (Arabic al-Jīzah) was founded in 642 AD opposite Fustat. Al-Maqrizi explained it as an Arameo-Arabic term meaning 'edge/side [of the valley]'; alternative scholarly hypotheses link it to Ancient Egyptian r-gs-ḥr ('beside the pyramid') or Middle Persian diz ('fortress').

b_abu_ghalib.first_mention_attestation: 1177 AD: Listed as 'Bū Ghālib' (بو غالب) in the Giza province in Ibn Mammati's Qawānīn al-Dawāwīn (al-Rawk al-Ṣalāḥī) and later as 'Abū Ghālib' in Ibn al-Ji'an's al-Tuḥfa al-Saniyya.
b_abu_ghalib.etymology_analysis: Abu Ghalib (Giza Governorate) is first attested in the 1177 AD Ayyubid cadastral survey (al-Rawk al-Ṣalāḥī) recorded by Ibn Mammati as Bū Ghālib, named after an otherwise unattested eponymous figure or founder; unattested by 867 AD.

b_busir.first_mention_attestation: c. 2450 BC (Old Kingdom Fifth Dynasty): Egyptian 'Per-Usir' (pr wsjr, 'House of Osiris'), attested in the Abusir Papyri and pyramid complex, passing into Greek 'Bousiris', Coptic 'Bousiri', and Arabic 'Būṣīr / Abū Ṣīr'.
b_busir.etymology_analysis: Busir / Abusir (Badrashin, Giza) is the direct phonological descendant of Ancient Egyptian pr wsjr ('House/Temple of Osiris') via Coptic Bousiri and Greek Bousiris. It served as a Fifth Dynasty royal necropolis and was also the site where the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was killed in 750 AD.

b_awjila.first_mention_attestation: c. 430 BC: Mentioned as 'Augila' (Αὔγιλα) by Herodotus in his Histories (Book IV) as a date-producing oasis visited by the Nasamones.

morphemes.translation: oasis name (linked in local tradition to Tebu 'Wajula' meaning 'low-lying land')

b_awjila.etymology_analysis: Awjila preserves its ancient Libyan name Augila (Αὔγιλα) attested since Herodotus (5th century BC) and later in Strabo, Ptolemy, and Procopius; conquered by Arab forces under 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd around 650 AD.

b_jalu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by name in pre-867 classical or early Islamic sources; documented in 19th-century travel accounts (e.g., 1872 description of Aujilah, Jalloo, and Leshkerreh) as a major Saharan caravan oasis.

morphemes.translation: oasis name of uncertain etymology (popularly linked to Arabic tajwāl 'wandering')

b_jalu.etymology_analysis: Jalu is a Cyrenaican oasis adjoining Awjila. The origin of the name Jalu is uncertain with no widely accepted linguistic explanation, and it is not attested in written sources by 867 AD.

b_jakharrad.first_mention_attestation: 1872 AD: Described in an 1872 European account alongside Aujilah and Jalloo under the form 'Leshkerreh' (al-Jikharra / Ijkharrah).

morphemes.translation: desert oasis northeast of Awjila and Jalu

b_jakharrad.etymology_analysis: Jikharra (Jakharrad / Ijkharrah) is the northeasternmost of the three Awjila-Jalu oases in Cyrenaica. While a modern study has proposed identifying an archaeological site there with Ptolemy's Dioskoron, the name Jikharra itself is unattested by 867 AD.

b_barqa-al-marj.first_mention_attestation: c. 560 BC: Ancient Greek 'Bárkē' (Βάρκη, Latin Barca), founded by Cyrenean exiles and the Libyan Barraci tribe according to Herodotus; Arabized as 'Barqah' (برقة) upon the 643–644 AD conquest.

morphemes.translation: Barca (originally a settlement of the Libyan Barraci tribe)
the meadows (later medieval name attested by al-Bakri in the 11th century)

b_barqa-al-marj.etymology_analysis: Barca (Greek Bárkē, Arabic Barqah) was an ancient Libyan and Greek city founded c. 560 BC and conquered by the Arabs in 643–644 AD, giving its name to the entire province of Barqah (Cyrenaica). The modern name al-Marj ('the meadows') arose later in the medieval period (attested by al-Bakri in the 11th century).

b_wadi_masus.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 classical or early Islamic sources; known in modern Libyan history from the Senussi zawiya (Zawiyat Msus) and battles in 1914 and World War II.

morphemes.translation: toponym of plausible Berber origin (compared to Beni Messous in Algeria; also Arabic masūs 'brackish/slightly fresh water')

b_wadi_masus.etymology_analysis: Wadi Masus / Zawiyat Msus is a desert valley and village southeast of Benghazi in Cyrenaica. The element Masūs is likely of Berber origin (or Arabic masūs 'brackish water'), but the place-name is unattested by 867 AD.

b_jabal_al-gharbi.first_mention_attestation: The Arabic geographic/administrative name 'al-Jabal al-Gharbī' ('the Western Mountain', referring to the Nafusa Mountains of Tripolitania, though misplaced in c_barqa in-game) is post-867 (district created in 1995/2007).
b_jabal_al-gharbi.etymology_analysis: Jabal al-Gharbi ('The Western Mountain') is the modern Arabic name for the Nafusa Mountains in northwestern Libya (and a modern Libyan district formed in 1995/2007). In the 8th–9th centuries, the range was known in Arabic sources as Jabal Nafūsa.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Early Islamic chronicles of the 8th-century Berber Revolt and the Ibadi Imamate of Jabal Nafusa (c. 740–750s AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: In 867 AD, the Nafusa Mountains were known by their tribal/Berber-derived name Jabal Nafusa rather than the later Arabic directional name al-Jabal al-Gharbi.

b_benghazi.first_mention_attestation: c. 1450 AD: Named 'Banī Ghāzī / Benghazi' ('Son of Ghazi') after the 15th-century Tripolitanian benefactor and saint Sidi Ghazi (Ibn Ghazi).
b_benghazi.eponym_details: Named after Sidi Ghazi (Ibn Ghazi, d. c. 1450), a Muslim saint and benefactor from Tripolitania; Benghazi literally means 'Son of Ghazi'.

morphemes.translation: Ghazi (personal name of the 15th-century saint Sidi Ghazi)

b_benghazi.etymology_analysis: Benghazi was named in the 15th century (c. 1450 AD) after Sidi Ghazi (Ibn Ghazi), a Tripolitanian saint/benefactor. The site was originally the ancient Greek colony of Euesperides (c. 525 BC), refounded in the 3rd century BC as Berenice.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Greek Pentapolis city Berenice / Hesperides (in-game: Benghazi)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 15th-century port of Sidi Ghazi fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to classical Greek Berenice.

older_name_by_867.notes: Euesperides (late 7th/6th c. BC) was relocated and refounded as Berenice in the 3rd c. BC, which persisted as a small town into the early Islamic period before being renamed Benghazi in the 15th century.

b_derna.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD: Ancient Greek 'Darnis' / 'Darne' (recorded in Ptolemy's Geographia and Roman/Byzantine ecclesiastical lists, e.g., Council of Sardica 347 AD), Arabized as 'Darnah' (درنة).

morphemes.translation: ancient city and episcopal metropolis of Libya Inferior (Marmarica)

b_derna.etymology_analysis: Derna (Arabic Darnah) is the direct phonological continuation of ancient Greek and Roman Darnis / Darne, a Hellenistic city and later Roman metropolis of Libya Inferior (Marmarica) attested from at least the 2nd century AD.

b_wadi_makhil.first_mention_attestation: c. 891 AD: Recorded as 'Wādī Makhīl' (وادي مخيل) by al-Ya'qubi in Kitāb al-Buldān as a town-like station with a congregational mosque, cisterns, markets, and a strong fort.

morphemes.translation: Makhil (desert station and wadi in Cyrenaica)

b_wadi_makhil.etymology_analysis: Wadi Makhil (modern Mechili / al-Makhili) is first attested in al-Ya'qubi's Kitāb al-Buldān (c. 891 AD), just after the 867 AD baseline, as an established Islamic desert station with a mosque, cisterns, markets, and fort.

b_marawa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 classical or early Islamic sources; documented in modern times as a pastoral and agricultural village in the Jabal al Akhdar region of Cyrenaica.

morphemes.translation: village in the Jabal al Akhdar, Cyrenaica

b_marawa.etymology_analysis: Marawa (Marawah) is a village in the Jabal al Akhdar highlands of Cyrenaica, Libya, between Marj and Lamluda. It has no attested historical record prior to 867 AD.

b_tobruk.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD: Ancient Greek 'Antipyrgos' (Ἀντίπυργος, Latin Antipyrgus) recorded in Ptolemy's Geographia and later as a Roman fortress and episcopal see (553 AD Council of Constantinople), evolving into Arabic 'Ṭubruq' (طبرق).
b_tobruk.etymology_analysis: Tobruk (Arabic Ṭubruq) is the direct phonological descendant of Ancient Greek Antipyrgos ('across from Pyrgos [in Crete]'), an ancient Greek colony and Roman frontier fortress attested since Ptolemy (c. 150 AD) and Justinian's 6th-century fortifications.

b_rashid.first_mention_attestation: 846 AD: Attested as Arabic 'Rashīd' (رشيد) in Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 846–885 AD), and fortified c. 853 AD following Byzantine raids.

morphemes.translation: guide / rightly guided (or from Coptic ti-Rashit)

b_rashid.etymology_analysis: Arabic Rashīd (Coptic ti-Rashit, ϯⲣⲁϣⲓⲧ) was established by the 9th century on the site of ancient Bolbitine; later Italian/French Crusaders adapted the name to Rosetta/Rosette ('little rose').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories (c. 450 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded on the site of the ancient Greco-Egyptian town of Bolbitine at the Bolbitinic mouth of the Nile.

b_damanhur.first_mention_attestation: c. 450 BCE: Attested in Imperial Aramaic as 'Temenkhūr' (תמנחור), from Ancient Egyptian 'pꜣ-dmỉ-n-Ḥr.w' ('the settlement of Horus').
b_damanhur.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic Damanhūr derives directly via Coptic p-Timinhor (ⲡϯⲙⲓⲛ̀ϩⲱⲣ) and Aramaic Temenkhūr from Ancient Egyptian pꜣ-dmỉ-n-Ḥr.w ('City/Settlement of Horus').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy, Geographica (2nd century AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Greco-Roman antiquity, the city was also called Hermopolis Mikra ('Little City of Hermes').

b_ramsis.first_mention_attestation: 641 AD: Recorded as 'Ramsīs' (رمسيس) at the time of the Islamic conquest of Egypt, giving its name to the Hawf Ramsis district in Beheira.
b_ramsis.etymology_analysis: Village in Itay al-Barud (Beheira Governorate) preserving the Ancient Egyptian royal name Rꜥ-ms-sw (Ramesses), continuously attested in Arabic administrative records since the 7th-century conquest.

b_minuf.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD: Attested as Greek 'Onouphis' (Ὀνουφις) in Ptolemy and as the bishopric of Onouphis/Panouf in 4th-century synods (c. 350 AD).
b_minuf.etymology_analysis: Arabic Minūf derives from Coptic Panouf (ⲡⲁⲛⲟⲩϥ, 'southern Panouf' / Minuf al-Ulyah), itself from Ancient Egyptian pꜣ-jw-nfr ('the good island'), Hellenized as Onouphis.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy, Geographica / 4th-century church synod lists
older_name_by_867.notes: Direct Egyptian and Greco-Coptic phonological ancestors of Minūf.

b_samannud.first_mention_attestation: c. 670 BCE: Attested in Assyrian records as 'Zabnuti' and in Greek as 'Sebennytos' (Σεβέννυτος) by Herodotus (c. 450 BCE) and Manetho (c. 290 BCE).
b_samannud.etymology_analysis: Arabic Samannūd derives via Coptic Jemnouti/Semenout (ϫⲉⲙⲛⲟⲩϯ) and Greek Sebennytos from Ancient Egyptian ṯb-(n)-nṯr ('city of the sacred calf').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Assyrian annals (7th century BCE) / Herodotus (c. 450 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Capital of the 12th Lower Egyptian nome and the 30th Dynasty (380 BCE).

b_burullus.first_mention_attestation: 431 AD: Attested as the bishopric of 'Paralus' (Πάραλος) at the Council of Ephesus (431 AD), and in Coptic as 'ti-Paralia' (Ϯⲡⲁⲣⲁⲗⲓⲁ).
b_burullus.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Burullus derives via Coptic ti-Paralia (Ϯⲡⲁⲣⲁⲗⲓⲁ) from Ancient Greek parálios/páralos ('coast, seaside'), originally a coastal port and bishopric on the Delta.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Council of Ephesus (431 AD) / Notitia Episcopatuum
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Coptic phonological ancestor of Arabic al-Burullus.

b_nastarawa.first_mention_attestation: c. 853 AD: Attested as 'Nastaruh' (نسترو / نستراوة) when its citizens strengthened its walls alongside Rashid and Alexandria after Byzantine raids on Damietta; Coptic 'Ništerōw' (ⲛⲓϣⲧⲉⲣⲱⲟⲩ).

morphemes.translation: island/settlement name in the Delta marshes

b_nastarawa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nastaruh / Nastarāwah derives from Coptic Ništerōw (ⲛⲓϣⲧⲉⲣⲱⲟⲩ), an island settlement in Lake Burullus (which Ibn Hawqal later called the Lake of Nastaruh).

b_ibyar.first_mention_attestation: c. 641 AD: Pre-Islamic town known in Coptic as 'Abior' / 'Biyār' (ⲁⲃⲓⲟⲣ), with its al-Umari Mosque dating back to the Islamic conquest of Egypt.
b_ibyar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ibyār derives from the plural of biʾr ('well'), rendered in Coptic as Abior (ⲁⲃⲓⲟⲣ) and calqued in Coptic as Hahshei (ϩⲁϩϣⲏⲓ, 'many wells').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Coptic-Arabic topographical tradition (pre-Islamic / 641 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Coptic renderings of the pre-Islamic settlement.

b_dumiyat.first_mention_attestation: 6th century AD (c. 550 AD): First historically attested as 'Tamiathis' (Ταμίαθις) by Stephanus of Byzantium and c. 605 AD by George of Cyprus.
b_dumiyat.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dumyāṭ (European Damietta) derives from Coptic Tamiati (ⲧⲁⲙⲓⲁϯ) and Greek Tamiathis (Ταμίαθις), traced to Ancient Egyptian Dmtjw ('inhabitants of the harbor').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Stephanus of Byzantium (6th century AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Coptic phonological ancestors of Dumyāṭ.

b_daqahla.first_mention_attestation: 641 AD: Known as Coptic 'Tkehli' (Ⲧⲕⲉϩⲗⲓ) at the Islamic conquest of Egypt, and attested as Arabic 'Daqahlah' (دقهلة) in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 AD).

morphemes.translation: toponym of the eastern Delta settlement

b_daqahla.etymology_analysis: Arabic Daqahlah derives directly from Coptic Tkehli (Ⲧⲕⲉϩⲗⲓ); it served as the capital of an Abbasid kūrah and later gave its name to Dakahlia Governorate.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Coptic topographical manuscripts / Islamic conquest records (641 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Direct Coptic ancestor of Arabic Daqahlah.

b_tinnis.first_mention_attestation: c. 420 AD: Attested in Late Antiquity as 'Thennesus' / 'Thennesos' (Θέννησος), Coptic 'Thennesi' (ⲑⲉⲛⲛⲉⲥⲓ), and Arabic 'Tinnīs' (تنيس) in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 AD).
b_tinnis.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tinnīs derives from Coptic Thennesi (ⲑⲉⲛⲛⲉⲥⲓ) and Greek Thennesos (Θέννησος), an island port in Lake Manzala (formerly Lake Tinnis) that flourished from the 9th to 11th centuries.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: John Cassian / George of Cyprus (c. 605 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Coptic phonological ancestors of Tinnīs.

b_bilbays.first_mention_attestation: 4th–5th century AD: Attested as the Roman-Byzantine bishopric of 'Phelbes' (Coptic Ⲫⲉⲗⲃⲉⲥ) in Augustamnica Secunda, and conquered as 'Bilbays' in 640 AD.

morphemes.translation: fortress city on the eastern Delta

b_bilbays.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bilbays (Bilbeis) derives from Bohairic Coptic Phelbes/Phelbēs (Ⲫⲉⲗⲃⲉⲥ/Ⲫⲉⲗⲃⲏⲥ), an ancient fortress town and Roman bishopric captured by Amr ibn al-As in 640 AD.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman-era bishopric lists of Augustamnica Secunda
older_name_by_867.notes: Coptic/Roman name of the site prior to Arabic Bilbays.

b_qalyub.first_mention_attestation: c. 690 AD: Attested in Coptic as 'Kaliōpe' / 'Kaliōps' (ⲕⲁⲗⲓⲱⲡⲉ / ⲕⲁⲗⲓⲱⲡⲥ) and in 7th-century chronicles of the Islamic conquest.

morphemes.translation: Calliope (personal name / Muse of epic poetry)

b_qalyub.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qalyūb derives via Coptic Kaliōpe/Kaliōps (ⲕⲁⲗⲓⲱⲡⲉ) from the Greek personal name Kalliópē (Καλλιόπη).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Coptic topographical tradition / 7th-century conquest chronicles
older_name_by_867.notes: Coptic phonological ancestor of Arabic Qalyūb.

b_faqus.first_mention_attestation: c. 20 BCE: Attested as Greek 'Phakousa' / 'Phakoussa' (Φάκουσα) by Strabo (Geographica) as capital of the Arabian nome.
b_faqus.etymology_analysis: Arabic Fāqūs derives from Greco-Roman Phakousa (Φάκουσα), itself reflecting the Ancient Egyptian prefix pꜣ- ('the') attached to the regional name (often linked to biblical Goshen/Gsm).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica (c. 20 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Roman phonological ancestor of Arabic Fāqūs.

b_um_shashoba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; modern Arabic Bedouin toponym for a gold-mining wadi area in Egypt's Southeastern Desert (Wadi Allaqi region).
b_um_shashoba.etymology_analysis: Arabic desert toponym of the Umm ('characterized by') type referring to an old gold-mining area in the Southeastern Desert near Wadi Allaqi, with no pre-867 AD attestation.

older_name_by_867.notes: Located in the ancient Wadi Allaqi mining region, but Um Shashoba itself is unattested <= 867 AD.

b_qusayr.first_mention_attestation: c. 1025–1030 AD: First attested under its Arabic name 'al-Quṣayr' (القصير) in the Fatimid chronicle Akhbār Miṣr by al-Musabbihi (and later Yaqut al-Hamawi in 1228 AD).

morphemes.translation: little fortress / small palace (diminutive of qaṣr)

b_qusayr.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Quṣayr ('the little fortress') is a medieval Fatimid-era name first attested c. 1025 AD, replacing the abandoned nearby classical port of Myos Hormos (Quseir al-Qadim, 8 km north).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Agatharchides (2nd c. BCE) / Strabo / Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
older_name_by_867.notes: Quseir al-Qadim, 8 km north of modern El Qoseir, was the Ptolemaic-Roman port of Myos Hormos (and Ancient Egyptian Tjau).

b_safaga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD under the name 'Safaga' (سفاجا); the modern port grew around phosphate mining in the early 20th century.

morphemes.translation: modern Red Sea coastal toponym of uncertain origin

b_safaga.etymology_analysis: Modern Arabic name Safāgā has no pre-867 AD attestation; the ancient settlement at the site was founded in the 3rd century BCE as Ptolemaic Philotera.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica / Pliny, Natural History 6.168
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded between 282 and 268 BCE by Satyrus and named Philotera in honor of the sister of Ptolemy II Philadelphus.

b_farama.first_mention_attestation: 640 AD: Captured as 'al-Faramā' (الفرما) during the Islamic conquest of Egypt, deriving from Coptic 'Peremoun' (Ⲡⲉⲣⲉⲙⲟⲩⲛ) and Ancient Egyptian 'pr-jmn'.
b_farama.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Faramā derives via Coptic Peremoun (Ⲡⲉⲣⲉⲙⲟⲩⲛ) from Ancient Egyptian pr-jmn ('House of Amun'), while the Greco-Roman name Pelusium (Πηλούσιον) refers to the muddy/marshy Pelusiac Nile mouth.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories (c. 450 BCE) / Book of Ezekiel 30:15
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in Classical antiquity as Pelusium and in Hebrew/Coptic as Sin.

b_warrada.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD; medieval Islamic waystation on the northern Sinai road (known for a Mamluk khan, near modern al-Khawaynat / Zaranik).

morphemes.translation: watering station / place of arrival (from root w-r-d, 'to arrive at water')

b_warrada.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Warrāda derives from the root w-r-d ('to come to water / arrive'), naming a medieval caravan station between al-Farama and al-Arish with no confirmed attestation <= 867 AD.

b_al-arish.first_mention_attestation: c. 846 AD: First mentioned under the Arabic name 'al-ʿArīsh' (العريش) in the 9th century (e.g., Ibn Khordadbeh's Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik).

morphemes.translation: huts / palm-branch shelters (or phonetic adaptation of Ariza)

b_al-arish.etymology_analysis: First attested as Arabic al-ʿArīsh in the 9th century, likely from Arabic ʿarš ('huts/shelters') built after the decline of Byzantine Rhinocorura, or from Hierocles's Ariza.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica / Strabo, Geographica
older_name_by_867.notes: In antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, the city was known as Rhinocorura ('cut-off noses').

b_firaun.first_mention_attestation: 1116 AD: First medieval historical/fortress attestations date to the Crusader (Ile de Graye, 1116 AD) and Ayyubid (Saladin, 1170 AD) periods; the Arabic name 'Jazīrat Firʿawn' is post-867.
b_firaun.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jazīrat Firʿawn ('Pharaoh's Island') is a post-867 medieval/modern name for a small granite island in the Gulf of Aqaba fortified in the 12th century.

older_name_by_867.notes: Some modern scholars tentatively identify the island with biblical Ezion-Geber, but this identification remains unconfirmed.

b_dahab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 AD under the Arabic name 'Dahab' (دهب); modern town grew from a Bedouin fishing village near Nabataean and Byzantine coastal ruins.
b_dahab.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dahab ('gold') refers to the golden sands of the Gulf of Aqaba coast; while Nabataean/Byzantine ruins exist nearby and some link it to biblical Di Zahab (Deut. 1:1), the Arabic name itself is unattested <= 867 AD.

older_name_by_867.notes: The identification with biblical Di Zahab (Deuteronomy 1:1) is scholarly conjecture rather than a confirmed attestation.

b_at-tur.first_mention_attestation: 13th century AD (c. 1200 AD): The town of At-Tur was founded in the 13th century near the ancient monastic/port site of Raythou (Raithu).
b_at-tur.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ṭūr derives from Aramaic ṭūrā ('mountain', i.e., Mount Sinai); while the regional oronym appears in early Islamic texts, the port town of At-Tur itself was founded in the 13th century near ancient Raithu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ammonius, Relatio (4th century AD) / Procopius
older_name_by_867.notes: At-Tur was founded in the 13th century near the ancient Christian monastic site and port of Raithu (medieval Raya).

b_stcatherine.first_mention_attestation: Built 548–565 AD as the Monastery of the Transfiguration / Burning Bush; the name 'Saint Catherine's' arose after Catherine's relics were associated with the site in the 9th–11th centuries (post-867 AD).
b_stcatherine.etymology_analysis: Founded by Emperor Justinian I (548–565 AD) as the Monastery of the Transfiguration; later renamed after Saint Catherine of Alexandria (d. c. 305 AD) following the medieval veneration of her relics there.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Procopius, De Aedificiis / Justinianic foundation (548–565 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Original 6th-century name of the monastery prior to its medieval renaming after Saint Catherine.

b_faran.first_mention_attestation: c. 150 AD: Attested as 'Pharan' (Φαράν) by Ptolemy (Geographica), and later as Arabic 'Fārān' (فاران) in Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 846 AD).

morphemes.translation: oasis and wadi in southern Sinai

b_faran.etymology_analysis: Arabic Fārān / Fayrān derives directly from Greco-Roman Pharan (Φαράν), a major early Christian oasis and bishopric in southern Sinai.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy, Geographica (2nd century AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Greco-Roman phonological ancestor of Arabic Fārān / Feiran.

b_qalat_jundi.first_mention_attestation: 1183 AD: Constructed by Saladin between 1183 and 1187 AD to guard the pilgrim and military road across Sinai.
b_qalat_jundi.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qalʿat al-Jundī ('Fortress of the Soldier') is a late 12th-century Ayyubid fortress built by Saladin in 1183–1187 AD.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Qal'at al-Jundi (Arabic 'Soldier's / Garrison Citadel' on Mount Sudr) (in-game: Knechtburch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Arabic fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Knechtburch.

b_tih.first_mention_attestation: c. 891 AD: Attested as a geographical region ('al-Tīh' / 'Bādiyat al-Tīh') in early post-867 Arab geographers such as al-Ya'qubi (Kitab al-Buldan, 891 AD) and al-Mas'udi.
b_tih.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Tīh ('the wandering', alluding to the biblical/Quranic 40 years of Israelite wandering in Sinai, Quran 5:26) names the central limestone plateau of Sinai.
